regions.name: Aravali Ranges
regions.biomes_note: Recorded from the species canon already places here -- hills and plains carry seven each, forest and mountains four. It was the last region with an `extent` drawn on the atlas and no biomes at all, which meant nothing could be laid out in it: `region_gedrosian_desert` had the same gap and was closed the same way. Advisory, as the schema says -- a field map's `seed_biomes` is still what the generator draws from, and a map here would want a cheap biome in the palette because hills, forest and mountains are all travel cost 2 or worse.

regions.name: Tethys Sky Routes & Floating Islands
regions.biomes_note: Deliberately empty. Sky species have no equivalent among the ten ground biomes, so everything filed here is held as lore and never placed on a tile.

field_maps.name: The Aravali Crossing
field_maps.arrival: The ranges come down to the water in steps of grey stone, and stop. Where they stop there is a rail-head, a shed, and a line of iron running out over the strait on trestles of pale timber. Two islands hang above the water along it, holding themselves up out of nothing anybody here will explain, and the rain that falls on their undersides falls upward. The far shore is a green smudge that is not Jambhudweepa. People cross. Nobody says much about the islands.

field_maps.name: North Dwarka
field_maps.arrival: Half of Dwarka is under the dust and the half that is not has been rebuilt twice on top of itself. The sea left inside living memory and nobody here treats that as a disaster or the gate as a wonder. Both are simply conditions, like weather, and the whole city is still arranged around a shoreline that stopped arriving.

field_maps.name: Lothal
field_maps.arrival: The delta takes a long time to become a city. Reeds, then reed-and-mud, then mud with brick in it, and then brick cut by someone who expected it to last. The tower is visible from a good way out, or the half of it still standing. Somebody has hung washing across the third storey.

lines: First light on the delta road. The cart keeps the pace of the ox, and you walk beside it.
Ahead, smoke rises from somewhere you cannot see yet.
A bedroll, a lamp, a staff, and a notebook a third full. You carry nothing else.
The rest of the notebook is the reason for the walk.
The delta takes a long time to become a city.
Reeds, then reed-and-mud, then mud with brick in it. Somebody has hung washing across the third storey.
The cart stops at the kilns, where people live because the kilns still hold heat.
Someone weaving a mat on the ground looks up, and moves over to make room.

field_maps.name: The Narmada Plateau
field_maps.arrival: The road up the scarp is the only part of the plateau anyone built. Everything above it was already here: black rock in steps a hundred feet high, holding a flat green country the sea never reached. They will tell you at the top that this is why the University is here. They are right, and it is not the whole reason.

points_of_interest.name: The Alms Step
points_of_interest.description: A domed temple on a high stepped plinth, and the names are on the step.
points_of_interest.arrival: Seven small spires stand around a dome that has split, and the doorway beneath them is a pointed arch with nothing behind it but dark. Lichen has taken the bottom two feet of everything. Dressed blocks lie scattered well out from the walls, far enough that they came off the top. The plinth it all stands on is pale stone, waist high, with steps down the front worn into dishes at the middle of each tread -- and along the plinth's face, cut small and shallow and running the whole length and round the corner, there are names. There are more names than a village.

points_of_interest.name: The Stepped Quarry
points_of_interest.description: Cut basalt in courses, and between two of the courses, a bed of something else.
points_of_interest.arrival: They quarried here for the halls and stopped when they hit a seam that would not dress. The seam is nine inches of pale ash between two floods of black rock, and it is full of small dead things lying in the order they died.

points_of_interest.name: The Black Pavement
points_of_interest.description: Basalt columns worn flat, and the ground everything here is built on.
points_of_interest.arrival: Hexagons underfoot, packed like a honeycomb and rubbed smooth by feet and salt. It goes under the wall, under the court, under the market. Somebody laid a city on top of it and never had to quarry a stone.

points_of_interest.name: The Bone Midden
points_of_interest.description: Where the city puts what it cannot eat, cannot burn, and does not want.
points_of_interest.arrival: Every settlement has a midden and this one has the usual fish spine and oyster shell and broken pot. It also has, at intervals, layers of something else — and the intervals are the interesting part.

points_of_interest.name: The Caravan Ground
points_of_interest.description: Where the road stops for the night, and has for longer than the road has made sense.
points_of_interest.arrival: The camp is on the wrong side of the ridge for shelter and the wrong distance from the water that is no longer there, and every caravan still stops here, because this is where you stop.

points_of_interest.name: The Cloud Stair

sub_locations.name: The Lower Flights
sub_locations.description: Cut into the scarp, wide enough for two, worn in the middle like any stair anyone ever used.

sub_locations.name: The Turn
sub_locations.description: Where the stair stops climbing the rock and starts climbing away from it. There is no rock under the last four steps and they are still there.

points_of_interest.description: A stair up the scarp that keeps going after the scarp stops.
points_of_interest.arrival: You can follow it with your eye until the cloud takes it, and the cloud is not always there, and it goes up past where the cloud is. Nobody at the University will say it is not a stair. They will say it has not been surveyed.

points_of_interest.name: The Drowned Dockyard
points_of_interest.description: Straight lines under the water, at what used to be a quayside.
points_of_interest.arrival: The basin was cut square and lined with fired brick, and salt water has been in it long enough that a reef has taken the corners. Fish that have never seen the open sea live in a harbour that no longer reaches it.

points_of_interest.name: The Drowned Seawall
points_of_interest.description: Three seawalls, one behind the other, each built when the last stopped working.
points_of_interest.arrival: You can wade the outermost at low water and stand on the innermost without getting your feet wet, and between them is four hundred years of a city agreeing, twice, that the sea had won that round.

points_of_interest.name: The Eastern Field
points_of_interest.description: Good flat ground, well watered, and nothing on it.
points_of_interest.arrival: Eight acres of level silt beside a channel that never runs dry, and not a stem on any of it. The camp plants here every spring out of stubbornness and takes nothing off it. Something came up out of the ground during the Shattering and has not gone back down.

points_of_interest.name: The Fang Bed
points_of_interest.description: Bones of the wrong animal in the wrong rock.
points_of_interest.arrival: A seam in the basalt full of bone, and the bone is all one kind of thing: heavy skulls with a pair of long teeth in the upper jaw and nothing like them since. They are lying in rock that formed after they should have been gone.

points_of_interest.name: The Far Landing
points_of_interest.description: The second island, and the last of Jambhudweepa.
points_of_interest.arrival: Another island, smaller, and the far shore visible past it as a green line that is not home. There is a bell on a post here, and a mark cut into the rail where somebody has been counting something.

points_of_interest.name: The First Pier
points_of_interest.description: The nearer island, where the line comes ashore in the air.
points_of_interest.arrival: The track runs out over nothing and then there is ground under it -- grass, low cushion-plant, a stand of aero-mangrove holding the edge together with its roots. Walk to the rim and the rain that is falling on the underside is falling the wrong way.

points_of_interest.name: The Gate Court

sub_locations.name: The Outer Court
sub_locations.description: Paving, a drain, and a low wall someone maintains. It looks like a yard because it is one.

sub_locations.name: The Threshold
sub_locations.description: Where the air stops being the same on both sides. You can stand with one hand in each and feel the difference at the wrist.

points_of_interest.description: A swept courtyard with a doorway in it that does not lead anywhere in this city.
points_of_interest.arrival: It is swept. That is the first thing, and it undoes most of what you were prepared for: somebody sweeps the gate court, the way somebody sweeps a threshing floor, because things come through and the mess has to go somewhere.

points_of_interest.name: The Glass Scar
points_of_interest.description: A seam of fused sand, running straight, where nothing should have been hot enough.
points_of_interest.arrival: Green-black glass, in a line you could follow at a walk, and under it sand that was never heated at all. Whatever did this did it fast enough that the heat had no time to go downwards. It runs out of the dry harbour and towards the gate, and nobody in the city will say whether that is a coincidence.

points_of_interest.name: The Grit Mill
points_of_interest.description: A mill in good repair, turning, with nobody in sight and nothing to sell to.
points_of_interest.arrival: White ceramic, rounded like a pot, braced in pale wood that somebody has oiled this year. A vine has been trained up one side rather than pulled off it. There are planters by the door with something flowering in them. The sails turn steadily in air that is not obviously moving, and inside, behind the door, the querns are running: you can feel it through the boards before you hear it. What comes out is black grit, bagged, stacked, more of it than anyone has carried down in a long time. Nobody answers.

points_of_interest.name: The Herders' Terraces
points_of_interest.description: Stone steps up a hillside, grazed by goats, described in the archive as ornamental.
points_of_interest.arrival: Two hundred steps of dry-laid stone, each one a little lower at the outer edge than the inner. Marn's goats are on them. The University's survey calls them a devotional feature and gives them a paragraph.

points_of_interest.name: The High Camp
points_of_interest.description: Two felt tents on the plateau, pitched where the grazing is and moved when it is not.
points_of_interest.arrival: Two round tents of stretched felt, guyed against a wind that does not stop, with stones on the ropes and a ring of hurdles round the whole of it. Marn's people winter lower down and are up here from the thaw. The University has a word for the terraces and no word for this.

points_of_interest.name: Kavik's Tower

sub_locations.name: The Lower Courses
sub_locations.description: Twenty-two storeys of red sandstone, of which four remain standing and the rest lie in roughly the order they fell.

sub_locations.name: The Stair Shaft
sub_locations.description: The stair survives because it was cut into the core rather than built against it. It goes up into daylight and down into water.

sub_locations.name: The Flooded Undercroft
sub_locations.description: Below the waterline the sandstone is cold and the carving is sharper, having been spared four hundred years of weather.

points_of_interest.description: Four storeys of red sandstone where the chronicles promise twenty-two.
points_of_interest.arrival: It did not topple. It sat down. The upper courses came straight through the lower ones and the whole thing settled into the delta mud like a foot into silt, which is why four storeys are still square and true and everything above them is a slope of dressed stone.

points_of_interest.name: The Kept Stones
points_of_interest.description: A wall somebody still repairs, around nothing anybody will name.
points_of_interest.arrival: Dry stone, a course or two higher than the weather would leave it, running round a shoulder of the range and enclosing a hollow with nothing in it. The gap that would be a gate has been closed with newer stone. There is no path to it and the grass at the foot is not grown over.

points_of_interest.name: The Lodestone Face
points_of_interest.description: An exposed core, and the only place the ore can be worked.
points_of_interest.arrival: A wound in the island's flank where something took a bite out of it, and the rock inside is black and faintly wrong. Grit stands on end where it has fallen. A dropped knife does not lie flat.

points_of_interest.name: The Long Archive

sub_locations.name: The Reading Floor
sub_locations.description: Long tables, north light, and the working copies -- which are copies of copies, and say so on the spine, which is more honest than most places manage.

sub_locations.name: The Sequence Stacks
sub_locations.description: Every measurement the University has taken, in the order it was taken. Four hundred years of rainfall, riverflow, birds arriving and birds leaving. It is beautiful and it is the whole problem.

sub_locations.name: The Unread Shelf
sub_locations.description: What came up the scarp already written and has never been transcribed, because nobody here can read it and nobody will admit that in writing.

points_of_interest.description: Four hundred and eleven years of measurements, kept perfectly.
points_of_interest.arrival: The stacks run back further than the lamps reach. Okhi says there are eleven thousand bound volumes and that she has personally copied four hundred of them, and then, without any change of tone, that she has no idea whether the oldest are true, only that they are old.

points_of_interest.name: The Camp in the Kilns
points_of_interest.description: Smoke, and washing strung between two courses of Harappan brick.
points_of_interest.arrival: Forty-odd people live in the kiln quarter, because the kilns were built to hold heat and still do. Nobody has repaired anything so much as leaned things against other things until they stopped falling. A child watches you from a doorway that used to be a flue.

points_of_interest.name: The Marsh Shrine
points_of_interest.description: Pale mangroves standing in a ring, and something at the centre that is not a tree.
points_of_interest.arrival: The Kia did not build the shrine so much as agree about it. A ring of ghost mangrove, a stone with a hollow worn into the top, and a great deal of water that is shallower than it looks if you know where to put your feet.

points_of_interest.name: The Narmada University
points_of_interest.description: Nine halls around a yard, and every one of them measuring something.
points_of_interest.arrival: It is smaller than the word suggests and busier than the quiet suggests. Nine halls, a yard with a rain gauge in it that has been read twice a day for four hundred and eleven years, and a great many people being careful. Nobody here is a fool. That turns out to matter more than the alternative would have.

points_of_interest.name: Nomad Ground
points_of_interest.description: Where the people who still cross put their tents.
points_of_interest.arrival: Felt tents on the shingle above the ford, guyed low, with the fire in the middle and the animals downstream of it. Nobody has pitched anywhere near the rail-head, which has a roof and a water butt and is a mile off.

points_of_interest.name: The Quiet Atelier
points_of_interest.description: A workshop of glass and benches, kept, and nobody in it.
points_of_interest.arrival: Glass panes in an iron frame, most of them whole, in a clearing that has been kept clear. Benches, seed trays in rows, a press, and jars along a shelf with the labels facing out. There is dust on all of it and not much.

points_of_interest.name: The Rail-Head
points_of_interest.description: Where the line begins, and where everybody waits for it.
points_of_interest.arrival: A shed, a water butt, a length of platform, and the iron running away north over the water on legs of pale timber. People sit on their bundles with the patience of those who have done this before. Nobody looks at the islands, which is its own kind of looking.

points_of_interest.name: The Salt Orchard
points_of_interest.description: Fruit trees dying at one end and something else doing well at the other.
points_of_interest.arrival: The orchard is half orchard. The seaward rows are salt-killed and standing, and through them, in the shade the dead trees still cast, something with the wrong leaf shape is doing extremely well.

points_of_interest.name: The Scale Shore
points_of_interest.description: Trackways in the stone, going into the sea.
points_of_interest.arrival: Three-toed prints in the black rock, a stride and a half apart, walking in a straight line toward water that was not there when they were made. They do not come back.

points_of_interest.name: The Second Gate
points_of_interest.description: Another doorway, out past the salt, that nobody sweeps.
points_of_interest.arrival: The same build as the Gate Court and none of the care: a frame of dressed basalt in a field of it, half-drifted with salt, and no path worn to it. It is not doing anything today.

points_of_interest.name: The Second Line
points_of_interest.description: A parallel embankment carrying nothing at all.
points_of_interest.arrival: An embankment running alongside the first, the same height and the same age, with no iron on it. Either it was lifted or it was never laid.

points_of_interest.name: The Silted Granary
points_of_interest.description: A grid of brick chambers filled to the brim with silt, and something growing out of them.
points_of_interest.arrival: The granary held the city's grain on raised platforms so the flood could not reach it. The flood has since reached it. What is remarkable is not that the chambers filled but that the crop came back on its own, red and thin, growing out of the tops of the walls.

points_of_interest.name: The Sunk Cutting
points_of_interest.description: A rail cutting the forest has closed over.
points_of_interest.arrival: The ground goes down between two banks and the canopy meets overhead, so it is a green tunnel with iron in the floor of it. Roots have come up between the sleepers and lifted them. A signal post stands in the middle with a tree grown through the frame.

points_of_interest.name: The Tide Market
points_of_interest.description: Trading twice a day, around a tide that decides when the floor is a floor.
points_of_interest.arrival: The market runs on the low water and stops on the high, so the day has two mornings and two evenings and everybody's sense of time is bent around it. Prices are quoted in what the tide will allow rather than in what a thing is worth.

points_of_interest.name: The Vedda Ford
points_of_interest.description: The old crossing, downstream of everything, still the shallowest water.
points_of_interest.arrival: Shingle on both banks and a bar between them you can wade at low water. There are stones set in the bed that are not river stones, worn round, laid a pace apart.

points_of_interest.name: The Walking Spring
points_of_interest.description: A spring the archive records at a fixed point, and a line of dead stonework saying otherwise.
points_of_interest.arrival: The water comes out of the hillside cold enough to hurt. Forty paces downslope there is a stone basin, dry, well made, and obviously built to catch exactly this. Forty paces further there is another.

points_of_interest.name: The Watch Stair
points_of_interest.description: Steps up the old wall, kept clear, with a good view of the court.
points_of_interest.arrival: Somebody keeps these steps clear of weed, and there is a worn patch at the top where people stand. They are not watching the sea from here.

lines.text: Terke moves the animals. I walk ahead of them and watch what else is walking.
Mostly I am not hunting. Mostly I am standing where a thing can see me, so it goes elsewhere and nobody has to do anything about it.
When I do take one it is one, and it is the one that was going to die this winter anyway. You learn to tell. That is most of the skill and none of the stories.
Hide, sinew, the long bones, the gut. Antler you find on the ground in spring and take nothing for at all, which is the best of it and costs only the walking.
The bow is sinew on timber. It tightens as it dries, which no rope does. So the animal gives you the thing that draws the bow that takes the animal. You can sit with that or you can not.
You have come from the spring. Everybody does, eventually, and asks me why it is not where the survey puts it. I say the survey is correct. I have been saying it for nineteen years.
Every post-hole on the plateau is in the survey, and every one was dug after the road. Nothing goes up on University ground that the survey has not seen.
I keep the ground book. The archive keeps what happened; I keep where it is allowed to happen. It is less interesting and I prefer it.
Before the first entry. -- Nineteen years, and I never once asked what the first page was written after.

npcs.name: The Asura-Tainted Princess
npcs.role: exile of the plateau, awake again

lines.text: Hi. You walk like somebody who came a long way to look at a stair. So did I, once. I have had a long time to think about it since.

These terraces could grow more than goats, if anybody asked them properly. My people are hungry in places you have not been yet. When you know what grows here, come and tell me, and I will tell you what I know about making it grow. And if you would be a friend of mine, cook me the Fourteen: fourteen bitter greens in one pot, counted. Nobody has cooked for me in a very long time.

Is that the Fourteen? -- Fourteen. You counted. Then we are friends, and friends drink something kinder than bitter greens afterwards. Ginger and ashwagandha root, cooked slow in whatever pot you have. My people brew it in copper up on the terraces. Now you can.

You have been up on the terraces. Look at the fall of the courses: a finger in a pace, along the hill and not down it. Whoever built them was feeding far more people than live up here now, and my people are some of what is left of them. Work out how they held the water and you will have worked out how we eat. That is what I know about making it grow.
Mask Family, yes. There is no family and there are no masks, so it is mostly a way of saying which brick I sleep under.

Everything I keep, I keep in something. That is the whole of the job. Clay for grain, because clay breathes a little and grain wants that. Wood for salt, because a fired jar sweats and salt draws the water straight out of the air to spite you.
We plant the eastern field every spring. My mother did. Her mother did. It is not stubbornness, it is that the ground is good and we cannot see what is wrong with it.
My grandmother walked to the shrine at night and came back dry. I have never known how and I have stopped asking whether it was true.
The niche in the stair. Something stood in it when my grandmother was small. She would not say what.

The north chamber is clear. The water was still falling under all that silt -- it never stopped, it only stopped being able to reach anything. We threshed in a morning what takes us four days. My mother would have called that a miracle and been wrong twice.

We are not moving in the spring. I have counted it four times and it keeps coming out the same, which is not something I am used to. Nine times I have moved this camp. My daughter will be the first of us to know what a place looks like in its second year.

Eight acres, sown from the granary wall. It will be a poor crop for three years and it will be a crop, which is three years better than a field we plant every spring out of habit. My mother planted it. Her mother planted it. Neither of them ever got anything back.
You have come a long way off the path.
It is a wall. It falls down. I put it back. That is the whole of it.
There is nothing in there. I have not been in there. My mother had not been in there.
You can write it down. Everybody writes it down. The stones do not mind.
Mind the walls. -- Not for your sake. For the rice. It grows in the ossu, the thin layer the flood left on top, and if you knock that off it there is nothing under it but brick.
Every autumn I cut it and every autumn it comes back. Nobody planted it. I have stopped asking who did.
You have been down the channel. I can see it on your feet. -- Six feet of fall, and I have been cutting rice off the top of it for twenty years like a goat.

npcs.name: Hasme
npcs.role: morol of the camp, keeper of the eastern field

lines.text: You are looking at the crust. Everybody looks at the crust. My mother said it was the Shattering's, and that the ground would come back when it chose. -- Eight acres, and it has not chosen. Ask anybody why and they will say poisoned, and not one of them could tell you what by.
I am the one they ask when a thing has to be decided about ground. Nobody has asked me about this field in a long time. Nobody wants it.
Rice? On the granary walls? -- I have walked past those walls every day of my life. Show me.
It runs when it runs. Sit down. You are not the first person to think looking at it will help.
No, it does not touch. Hand's width, whole way over. You get used to the quiet or you walk, and there is no walking.
The black stuff under the rail is the same as the islands. Same rock. It wants to be up, so up is where it stays, and we lay iron on it and call that a road.
Bolt holes and no bolts. My grandmother said her grandmother said it was built to come up again. Nobody has ever taken it up.
Look at the two headlands. Same stone, same tilt, same courses. It was one hill. The middle of it is those two things hanging over the water, and you are about to ride across the gap where it broke.
The glass is hers. I only keep it swept and the trays turned.
She is not coming this month. She sends soil, and I plant it, and I write down what comes up. Mostly nothing comes up.
That is the point of it -- the nothing. If you only sow good dirt you learn what you already knew. She wants the ground that has stopped, and a list of what will still take in it.

Physic first, because sick people cannot wait for a harvest. Neem for the skin, brahmi for the head, haritaki for everything nobody has a name for. Then the grasses, because grass holds a slope. Then whatever will feed anyone.
The lotus in the falling-up water keeps its warmth after it is picked. I have not worked out what that is for. She will know, or she will write to somebody who does.
Hear that? Strike the flag by the well and it rings hollow. Tan, the drivers call it -- the road's note. Where the ground rings like that, the road goes round.
Every stall on this rise pays the well a skin of water a season. I keep the well. So they pay me, and I keep the well. It is not complicated.
University people draw me a straight line across the basin every year and tell me I am losing a day. I give them a skin of water for the walk and they come back the long way.
So you walked it. -- Now you know why nobody here needs telling.

npcs.name: Kunch
npcs.role: road singer, up on a bird

lines.text: You will hear me before you see me and that is the arrangement. Cane, cut to length -- this one is the water note, this one is two fields of walking, this one I do not use because it sounds like somebody being unwell. Cut them long and take them down to the note; they only tune one way. Bind them at the grip or you are carrying three sticks.

Her name is not your business and she would not answer to it anyway. Nine feet of bad opinion and the only animal on this delta that can see over the reeds, which between us is the whole of why I am up here and not down there with my feet wet.
Nobody pays me. People feed me, which is not the same and is more reliable. A song does not go off.
The shrine, yes. I do not go in and I do not sing near it. Not for any reason I can give you -- the cane sounds wrong there, flat where it should not be flat, and I have stopped arguing with it.
The steps? The steps have always been the steps. Good grazing, stays green late. You are the first person to walk up them looking at them.

Comb it, do not cut it. The winter coat comes away in your hand in spring and the animal is happier for it. It spins rough and it stays warm wet, which up here is the only question anybody is actually asking about cloth.
Khet. Not step -- khet. It means the water is held. I do not know why we call them that, we just do.
We lose one a year to the millet and we have always lost one a year to the millet. If you are telling me that is a choice and not a weather, I will need to sit down.

So the spring moved and the archive did not. I have been grazing off the old mark my whole life and telling myself the water was unreliable. The water is fine. It is the mark that is wrong, and a mark is a thing a person put there.

Bhar. Not the weight -- the weight is the weight, anybody with a rope knows the weight. Bhar is what she has agreed to carry today, and it is always less, and arguing about the difference is how a driver gets a foot broken.

Six courses of the hall came up this road on her mother. They will tell you up there that the stone was quarried in such a year by such a hand. The stone was quarried by a hand and moved by an animal, and only one of those is written down.
She drinks at the spring and I do not hurry her. It is an hour. I have had that hour every second day of my life and I would not sell it.

Nine inches, every course, all the way up. She sets them down to a finger and I have never once told her how far to lower. Somebody up there measured it afterwards and wrote the number in a book, and the number was already in the animal.
Careful in the cutting. The sleepers go through where the roots have had them.
Chairs, plates, bolts. Good iron, better than anything anybody smelts now, and there is a hundred miles of it under that green.
Two lines. Nobody believes me till they walk the second bank. Two lines, and one lifted before the other stopped.
What ran on it? Something that needed doubling. That is all the iron will tell you and I have asked it a lot.
Eleven thousand volumes. I have copied four hundred. I do not know if the oldest are true, only that they are old, and that is not nothing.

Soot, gum, and the patience to let it dry properly. Everyone wants to write with it wet. -- The leaf takes a scored line better than it takes ink, which is why the old books are cut and not painted. Eleven thousand volumes and I know how every one of them was made.

Nothing here was ever on a shelf first. The oldest volumes came up out of the ground in jars, sealed, and the jars are the only reason there is anything to copy -- so a copyist learns to fire one before she learns to cut a letter. And an awl: you prick the leaf, you thread the cord through, and the book is a book. Bone, a deer's shin for choice. Mine is older than Vessa.
There is a shelf I dust and cannot read. Thirty years. If you learn what is on it I would like to be told, and I would like it told to me before it is told to the halls.
No. Somebody stays. You have all found the thing that is wrong with this place and you are all leaving with it, and the eleven thousand volumes are still here and still need copying.

One bird, two entries, thirty years apart, and I have dusted both shelves. Nobody rereads. I am going to start at the oldest and work forward, and I expect it will take the rest of my life, and I would rather know.
I keep the inner wall and I sweep the court. They are the same job to me: something arrives, and it has to go somewhere.

Husk, not reed. Reed rope on a wall by the sea is a rope you replace twice a year and eventually you are not mending the wall, you are mending the rope. Lay it in three strands against the twist and it will still be there when I am not.
In mist, yes. Not every mist. You will want the stair and three days, and you will be the first person to sit them who was not being paid.
No. My father rebuilt this wall and I have rebuilt it and my son will. You are asking me to leave a job that is not finished, and it is never going to be finished, and that is not a reason.

Three strands, and you laid them against the twist. -- Then I can get to the outer course alone, and I have wanted to get to the outer course alone for eleven years. Sit down. A span is two anchors and a line you are willing to hang from, and the third part is the only one that takes any nerve.
You are standing on it. Everybody stands on it. It goes under the whole town.
Hexagons. All the way down as far as anybody has dug, and nobody has dug far, because why would you.
The bone seam is up by the hill. Big teeth, two of them, top jaw. Not a fish and not a cat.
And the bird tracks are in the same rock, down at the shore. I have shown a dozen people and you are the second to go and look at both.
Everything the city cannot use comes to me eventually. Most of it is fish. Some years it is not.

Everyone thinks I am looking for something. I am looking at *how things break*. Bone breaks along the grain and shell does not, so bone makes a point and shell makes a bead. Here -- drill it wet, and go slower than you want to.
You want the thin layers. My mother showed me where they are, and hers showed her, and none of us has ever been asked about them before today.
The orchard? The orchard is finished. I would rather you told me something about it that I can do than something about it that is true.

Layers, yes. My mother knew where the thin ones were and I know, and neither of us knew why. It is not a thing that happened to Dwarka. It is what Dwarka is, and we already had a word for it and a place to put the bones.
Animals will not go on the iron. Would you? It hums.
We cross at the shingle. Always the shingle. My mother crossed at the shingle and hers.
There are stones down there, set in the bed. Not ours. They were there when we started coming and we use them, so.
The rail people ask why we do not ride. We ask why they wait.
You will want the basin at night, after rain. The water goes silver and they come up. Ask me why and I will tell you I do not know.

A weir is a fence that does the fishing while you are asleep. Cane, set slant to the current, and a rope through the tops so the whole run comes up together. What it catches it catches -- you do not get to choose, and that is why I never say I caught anything in particular.
My grandfather had a word for it. Thal-something. He is dead and I have half of it.
The far banks I cannot work. Water looks the same everywhere out there and it is not the same, and I have a family.

I can see the bottom. Do you understand what I am telling you -- I have set nets by feel for nineteen years and this morning I looked through a piece of the eastern field and saw the channel bed. The field nobody could plant. It was giving us this the whole time.

Bekh has it written down. Four months a year I could not fish and now I can, and the reason is a kiln and a mill and a piece of glass, none of which is mine. I do not entirely follow it. I am not going to argue with a full net.

npcs.name: Tolla
npcs.role: head herder, dada of the high grazing

lines.text: A goat carries what it agreed to carry and not a handful more. Bhar, we say -- a load with consent in it. Put a thing on a goat without asking and it will lie down in the road and be right.
The top step is the goats' in the dry months. It always has been. The University calls it ornamental, and I let them.
The wind comes over the edge up here like a hand. It took my father's tent. It has taken better things than that.
You stood in it. On purpose. -- Then you know it is not only taking.
Three kilns, every year, and every year the same three. I have stopped minding. It is something to do in spring.

You are sleeping on the ground, I can see it from here. Sit. -- No, like that, butt the reeds against the frame, do not weave the ends in. The ends are where a mat goes first. Three of those and you have a floor. Six and you have a wall.
After the flood? Nobody cuts reed after the flood. -- No, I am listening. Say it again.

You were right about the wind. We turned the spring kiln to face the plateau and it fired in a day, on half the reed. Half. I have been cutting twice what I needed since I was fourteen and nobody ever stood in the doorway and looked at which way the smoke went.

Bekh says we are staying. So I am going to put a proper roof on the kiln shed, the kind you build when you expect to be under it. It will take three weeks and there is no reason to hurry, which is the strangest part.

Is that one of mine? -- It is one of yours. Good. Then stop sleeping on the bare ground: oiled cloth over the mat, rolled and strapped, and it does not matter what the night does. I made my first one at eleven and I have been dry ever since.

npcs.name: Ushi
npcs.role: keeper of the salt orchard, morol of the market's growers

lines.text: Water them from the landward end, always. My grandmother said so and she was right about everything else. -- The market calls that uvai: a thing remembered by somebody who is not here to be asked why.
Every surveyor who comes down from the plateau tells me it is the salt. It has been salt here since before the orchard. The trees did well in it for sixty years.
I am the one the growers send to the market when there is an argument about water. There is always an argument about water.
Fever-root. -- I have been pulling it up for ten years and calling it a weed. It is not a weed. It is winning.
You will want the rain series. Everyone wants the rain series. Read the first ten years of it and then come and tell me what you think we are measuring against.

Nobody teaches this because everybody assumes you know. Cut the reed at a slant, recut it every few lines, and do not mourn it -- a stylus is a thing you lose. The tally is different. Notch it, split it, and neither of you can lie afterwards.

I have written it three times and withdrawn it three times. Not because they would be angry. Because they would ask what the pre-Shattering figure was, and there isn't one, and that is the end of the conversation.
My grandmother's people counted years by what happened in them. The halls would call that anecdote. It is also the only record that reaches back past the wound.

happenings.title: The tower, standing
happenings.prose: You dream of Kavik's tower before it sat down: all twenty-two storeys, dry ground to the horizon, and the stair going up through the middle of it. You climb. At shoulder height there is a niche in the stair wall, and something in it is looking out at you with a face that is not a face. You wake before you reach it.

choices.label: Write it down before it goes
choices.line: You write down the niche and the height of it, by feel, in the dark. In the morning the page is mostly scrawl, but the height is legible: shoulder height, on the stair.

choices.label: Lie still and let it fade
choices.line: You lie still and let the tower go back to rubble. What stays is the niche, and the feeling of being looked at by something that was meant to be there.

happenings.title: Where you stop
happenings.prose: A caravan is already unloading when you arrive: donkeys hobbled, water skins stacked, a fire started in a ring of stones blackened by a great many fires before it. You ask the drover why they camp here, on the wrong side of the ridge and a long walk from the well. She looks at you as if you had asked why the sun comes up in the east. This is where you stop, she says. Everybody stops here.

choices.label: Ask who stopped here first
choices.line: Her grandfather's caravan stopped here, she says, and his grandfather's before that. Nobody remembers a reason. You look at the line the road takes into camp and wonder what it is following.

choices.label: Stop here too
choices.line: You unroll your bedding beside theirs. It is a bad place to camp, exposed and far from water, and everybody in it sleeps well, because this is where you stop.

happenings.title: Counting years
happenings.prose: An old herder is resting on the terrace wall while her goats work the slope below. She tells you, without being asked, that she was born in the year the goats went up early, married in the year of the long frost, and that her mother used to say the water had walked in the year before she was born. Nobody on the plateau counts years any other way, she says, except the people in the halls, and they only started when everything broke.

choices.label: Ask what the water's year is called
choices.line: She says it twice, slowly, so you have it: anu-shivit, the year it walked. The spring has a name for its own last move, and nobody wrote it down in a hall.

choices.label: Sit with her a while
choices.line: You sit on the wall while she names the years back to her grandmother's. Somewhere in there is the year the water walked -- anu-shivit, she calls it -- and it is older than the halls' first page.

homesteads.name: The pump on the long way

grounds.name: The orchard's dry end
grounds.prose: The landward rows of the salt orchard, on firm ground above the crust, where the trees are still doing well and the wind comes in off the basin without anything in its way. Ushi waters them from this end, always, and does not intend to stop.

worries.says: The trees are dying from the sea end. You are going to tell me it is the salt. Everybody from up the coast tells me it is the salt.
worries.hint: She is not asking to be told. She knows it is not the salt, and she is waiting to see whether you have looked at what is doing well where the trees are not.
worries.not_that: That is the salt answer again, in better words.
worries.eased: Fever-root. Taking the ground a finger at a time, and making it no good for anything else. -- I said it was not the salt. Nobody listens to the one who does the watering.

worries.says: And the sea will not be back. It has left before and it will leave again, and a thing built for it coming back is a thing that will be wrong in my lifetime.
worries.hint: She is not frightened of the sea going. She wants to know you have understood that it goes -- the midden says so, or anybody who picks it.
worries.not_that: That does not tell me you know what happens here.
worries.eased: Yes. Layer on layer of it, and a word for it, and a place for the bones. You have read it. Good.

worries.says: And you are from the plateau, or from the delta, or somewhere they measure things. The orchard does not need measuring.
worries.hint: She wants you to have learned something here rather than brought it: a word of the market's, or somebody of Dwarka's to speak for you.
worries.not_that: That is where you are from. I asked what you have learned here.
worries.eased: You have been listening, then. That is rarer than you would think.

grounds.agrees: Put it at the dry end, then, and turn the pump to the landward well -- the old one, the one my grandmother used. And pull the fever-root on your way past. Every time.

grounds.name: The caravan rise
grounds.prose: A low rise above the Caravan Ground, where the road stops for the night beside a well older than the road. The flagstones round the well ring hollow if you strike them, and every stall on the rise pays Jarro for the water.

worries.says: The road goes the long way round the basin. You want to build on the long way. Tell me why it is long, and I will tell you whether you can.
worries.hint: He knows why. He is not asking you to find out; he is asking whether you already have. Somebody who had walked the road as it goes would know what it goes round.
worries.not_that: That is a University answer. They draw a straight line and come back the long way.
worries.eased: Water. It goes where the water was, and the water was here. -- Nobody needs to be told that twice.

worries.says: And a pump. For what -- the harbour? There is no harbour. The sea is not coming back, whatever they tell each other in the gate court.
worries.hint: He wants to know you have stopped waiting for the sea. The walls could tell you that, or the market's slates, or the man who keeps them.
worries.not_that: You are still building for the sea. It has gone.
worries.eased: Later every year. It is on the slates, and the walls say it, and you have read them both. Then you are pumping from the well, like a sensible person.

worries.says: And the rise pays the well. Every stall pays. A pump on my rise pays as well, or the drivers ask why they do.
worries.hint: He does not want paying so much as he wants to be seen to be paid. Anything the road would trade for, shown to him, would do.
worries.not_that: That is not something a driver would take for water.
worries.eased: That will do. Keep it -- I only wanted it said in front of the drivers that you would.

grounds.agrees: Build it by the well, then. Where the flag rings. And when it turns, the first skin is the well's -- which is to say mine.

stages.name: Lay the footing
stages.prose: Dressed sandstone in a ring on the firm ground, packed with husk against the wind, and a scaffold of old harbour spars lashed round it. Somebody you helped brought a cart for the stone and said it was going that way anyway.

stages.name: Raise the tower
stages.prose: A lattice of mangrove poles, guyed with husk hawser laid the way Pell lays it, three strands against the twist. From the top you can see the whole basin, the road going the long way round it, and exactly what it goes round.

stages.name: Hang the vanes, and fill the still
stages.prose: Vanes of husk matting on a ring of spokes, plaited the way the harbour once plaited its sails, that turned the first morning and lifted water the first afternoon. Beside the pump a still-house on a sandstone footing, salt-glass over shallow trays, where the sun takes the brine and leaves the water, and date palms set in the first beds of it -- offsets, carried up from the last grove by the market, because a date palm is grown from its mother and not from its stone.

homesteads.settled: They came up from the market at evening -- growers, a driver or two, somebody's grandmother -- and nobody said it was a place yet. The vanes turned. The still dripped. By dark there was a lamp in the glasshouse and a queue at the well, and Jarro was taking nothing from anybody, and pretending he was.

homesteads.name: The mill among the trees

grounds.name: The Eastern Field
grounds.prose: Eight acres of good silt beside permanent water, trees standing close around three sides, and nothing growing on it but a white crust after a dry week. Hasme keeps it. Nobody has asked her for it in a generation, because nobody has wanted it.

worries.says: It is poisoned. My mother sowed it and my aunts sowed it, and it took every seed and gave back salt. You want to build on ground that eats what you put in it.
worries.hint: She is not frightened of the field. She is frightened of being told again that it will grow, by somebody who has not looked at why it did not.
worries.not_that: That is a fine thing, and it is not the field. Tell me about the field.
worries.eased: Salt. Coming up from underneath. -- And the red rice on the granary walls does not mind it. Nobody told me that in forty years. Go on.

worries.says: And then the camp moves. Every third winter we move, because the stores run out before the spring does. Nobody builds for a camp that leaves.
worries.hint: She is counting winters the way Bekh counts stores. Somebody who knew why the camp moves could tell her whether it still has to.
worries.not_that: That does not keep anybody fed in the fourth month.
worries.eased: Not moving in the spring. Bekh said so, and I did not believe her, and now you have it written down.

worries.says: And you are not of the delta. I do not say that against you. I say it because the field will still be here when you have gone on.
worries.hint: She wants to know you will be spoken for when you are not standing here: by the delta's own words, or by one of the delta's own people.
worries.not_that: That is yours. I asked what is ours.
worries.eased: Well. Somebody here will answer for you, then. That is all I wanted.

grounds.agrees: Build it, then. Put the mill where the trees are, so the wind comes over them clean, and sow the red rice first. If it does nothing for three years I shall say I told you so, and I shall help you cut it anyway.

grounds.name: The granary's edge
grounds.prose: Dry ground along the granary's north wall, above the silt, where the stone channel comes in. Drel cuts the red rice off the walls every autumn and has come to think of the whole building as his.

worries.says: This rice is mine to cut. I cut it every autumn. You build here and every fool in the camp comes to help themselves.
worries.hint: He is not greedy so much as afraid of there being too little. Somebody who knew where else it would grow would take the fear out of it.
worries.not_that: That does not put rice in my basket.
worries.eased: It will grow in the eastern field? In salt? -- Then there is enough for the fools as well. Fine.

worries.says: And the walls. The granary came down once. Put a mill against it and it comes down again, on top of my rice.
worries.hint: He thinks the granary fell. Somebody who had followed the old channel through it would know what actually stopped.
worries.not_that: Walls do not care about that.
worries.eased: It did not fall. It silted. -- The channel still runs. I have heard it and thought it was the marsh. Build your mill, then, and clear the north chamber while you are about it.

grounds.agrees: Go on, then. Where the channel comes in. And the first sack off the new mill is mine.

stages.name: Lay the foundation
stages.prose: A ring of fired clay blocks, knee-high, with the first course of the wall begun on it, and a scaffold of poles lashed round it. Somebody you helped carried half the clay and would not hear of being thanked.

stages.name: Raise the tower
stages.prose: The tower is above the trees now, still in its scaffolding, a hoist at the top lifting one block at a time. From the top course you can see the camp's smoke and the line of the channel, and which way the wind comes over the canopy.

stages.name: Hang the sails, and sow the rice
stages.prose: Four sails of fired clay on bamboo spars, and they turned the first afternoon. Beside the mill, a glasshouse of salt-glass panes over the seedlings, and the first red rice from the granary walls in the ground below it.

homesteads.settled: They came along the path at evening with bundles and a rolled mat, and lit the lamps. Nobody made a speech. The mill turned over the trees, and the glasshouse was warm inside, and it was, without anybody deciding it, a place people lived.

homesteads.name: The mill at the edge of the survey

grounds.name: The yard's east edge
grounds.prose: Level ground past the ninth hall, where the University's yard runs out into grass and the scarp wind comes across unbroken. It is in the survey as empty, has been for four hundred years, and Ardhi keeps it that way.

worries.says: There is no record of anything standing on the east edge. Four hundred years and not a post-hole. Nothing goes up where the record says nothing was.
worries.hint: She trusts the archive the way other people trust ground. Somebody who knew where the record begins could show her what it cannot have seen.
worries.not_that: That is not in the record, so I cannot weigh it.
worries.eased: It starts at the wound. -- Then 'nothing was here' only ever meant 'nothing was here after'. Very well. I shall have to write that down somewhere I will see it.

worries.says: And a glasshouse wants water, and the survey puts the spring a mile from the east edge. It has not moved in four hundred years.
worries.hint: The survey is exact about where the spring was on one day. Somebody who had followed the dead stonework up the hill would know where it is now.
worries.not_that: The spring is where the survey says. Everything is.
worries.eased: Three moves. And the survey caught it on the day of the second. -- It is closer than a mile, then. I shall not be the one to tell the archive.

worries.says: And nobody on the plateau builds. Everything above the scarp was already here. We measure it. That is what the University is for.
worries.hint: She says it as if it were a law of the ground. The terraces would argue, if anybody could read them, or if anybody had asked what they water.
worries.not_that: That is a thing somebody found. I said built.
worries.eased: Construction records. On the unread shelf. -- Then somebody built all of it, and we have been measuring their work and calling it the weather.

grounds.agrees: Build it on the east edge. I shall enter it in the ground book on the day it goes up, which will make it the first thing in four hundred years the University has watched being built rather than found.

grounds.name: The top terrace
grounds.prose: The highest step of the terraces, flat and dry, with the scarp dropping away beyond it and the whole plateau below. The goats graze it in the dry months. The wind comes over the edge hard enough to lean on.

worries.says: The top step is the goats' in the dry months. Build on it and they go without. I will not have that.
worries.hint: He is counting fodder. Somebody who knew what else grows up here -- a thing the University's lists call poison -- would take the count off his mind.
worries.not_that: That does not feed a goat.
worries.eased: The millet. The bitter one. -- Soak it, you say, and it is food. The goats have been telling me that for years and I have been pulling them off it.

worries.says: And the wind. It comes over the edge like a hand. It took my father's tent. You want to hang sails in that?
worries.hint: He thinks of the wind only as the thing that takes. Somebody who had stood in it on purpose, and learned how it stands, would know what it could turn.
worries.not_that: The wind does not care about that.
worries.eased: Lift. It does not blow across, it stands up the scarp. -- Then it will turn a mill all year and never take it. Fine. Fine.

worries.says: And you are down from somewhere. Everybody up here is from up here, even the University, even if it will not say so.
worries.hint: He wants you spoken for up here: in the herders' own words, or by somebody the plateau owes.
worries.not_that: That is yours. I asked what is ours.
worries.eased: Somebody up here will answer for you. Then you are from up here, as far as the goats are concerned.

grounds.agrees: The top step, then, with its back to the edge. Sow the bitter millet on the step below it, and the first flour off the mill is the goats'. They were here first.

stages.name: Lay the footing
stages.prose: Squared basalt from the stepped quarry in a ring on the level ground, bedded in bast against the frost, and a scaffold of poles. Somebody you helped brought the stone down on a straight-tusk and would not say whose idea it was.

stages.name: Raise the tower
stages.prose: A tower of cane lashed with goat-hair cord, twisted by hand on the terraces the way Marn twists it, light enough that the lift nearly takes it off the scaffold. From the top course you can see the terraces all the way down, and see that they are a farm.

stages.name: Hang the sails, and sow the millet
stages.prose: Four sails of scraped hide on cane spars, set into the lift, turning before they were fully tied. Beside the mill a glasshouse, warm against the plateau's cold nights, with the bitter millet in trays under it, soaking, the way Marn says. And on the mill's far side a hive on a thatched stand, because the terraces flower in the rains and somebody up here should have the good of it.

homesteads.settled: They came up from the halls and down from the grazing at the same hour, which has not happened on the plateau in living memory, and stood about in the lamplight not quite knowing who should speak first. Nobody did. The mill turned on the lift. Somebody wrote it down.

sayings.name: A pause between two horizons
sayings.text: A camp is only a pause between two horizons.

sayings.name: Nobody leaves their ancestors
sayings.text: A traveller may leave a house. No one leaves their ancestors.

sayings.name: Before there were kingdoms
sayings.text: Before there were kingdoms, there were fires. Before there were roads, there were feet.

sayings.name: Carry the names
sayings.text: Leave the stones behind. Carry the names.

sayings.name: Count the fires
sayings.text: Count not the miles beneath your feet. Count the fires that welcomed you.

sayings.name: The dawn belongs to the traveller
sayings.text: The dawn belongs neither to the city nor the wilderness. It belongs to the traveller.

sayings.name: Dawn has opened the road
sayings.text:
Dawn has opened the road.
Rise.
Wake the oxen.
Gather the water.
Fold the tents.
The night has carried us this far.
The light will carry us farther.

sayings.name: The fire travels with us
sayings.text: The road is long, but the fire travels with us.

sayings.name: What each thing gives
sayings.text:
Dawn gives the road.
The river gives direction.
The ancestors give memory.
Ṛta gives meaning.

sayings.name: Four things we carry
sayings.text:
When we leave, we carry four things.
Fire,
water,
the seed,
and the names of the dead.
The road may take the first three from us.
It cannot take the fourth.
For the ancestors have already walked ahead.
We are only following their footprints.

sayings.name: Whoever knows the stars
sayings.text: Whoever knows the stars need not fear the empty plain.

sayings.name: The mountains do not move
sayings.text: We cross the mountains because the mountains do not move.

sayings.name: Our road was written
sayings.text: Our road was written before our mothers and fathers were born.

sayings.name: Remember the rivers
sayings.text:
Remember the rivers.
Remember the river behind us,
and the river before us.
Remember where the oxen drank.
Remember where the mothers rested.
Remember where the dead were given to the earth.
A people may forget a king.
A people must never forget a river.

sayings.name: The river leaves its birthplace
sayings.text: The river leaves its birthplace, yet it does not cease to be a river.

sayings.name: Another road
sayings.text: The rivers are not the road's end. They are another road.

sayings.name: Who remembered the road
sayings.text:
The road was here before us.
Our mothers and fathers walked it.
Theirs walked it before them.
We walk it now.
Do not ask who made the road.
Ask who remembered it.
For when the stones disappear
and the grass covers the footprints,
the road remains
inside the memory of the people.

sayings.name: Ṛta is the road
sayings.text: Ṛta has no road. It is the road.

sayings.name: The bones are listening
sayings.text: Walk lightly. The bones beneath the earth are listening.

sayings.name: The land remembers
sayings.text: The land does not belong to those who stay. It remembers those who pass.

sayings.name: The next fire
sayings.text: Where the old fire burned, we shall make the next fire.

sayings.name: The sea remembers their names
sayings.text: The mountains remember our ancestors. The sea remembers their names.

sayings.name: The stars remember the way
sayings.text: We follow the stars because the stars remember the way home.

sayings.name: The tent has no roots
sayings.text: The tent has no roots, but the people do.

sayings.name: The Walking Song
sayings.text:
Do not ask where the road ends.
Ask what it has taught your feet.

Our mothers and fathers crossed the salt plains.
Theirs crossed the mountains.
Before them, others followed the rivers south.

We carry no kingdom upon our backs.
Only fire, water, seed, and memory.

When the grass calls, we rise.
When the sky changes, we turn.
When the old road disappears,
we become the road.
sayings.attribution: The Walking Song, attributed to the first Vedda

sayings.name: The wind has no house
sayings.text: The wind has no house. Neither should the memory of a people.

sayings.name: The world remembers every footstep
sayings.text: The world remembers every footstep, even when the sand forgets.

sayings.name: They carried memory
sayings.text: The first people carried no maps. They carried memory.

sayings.name: We follow the world
sayings.text: We do not wander. We follow the world as it moves.

sayings.name: When the grass dies
sayings.text: When the grass dies, we rise. When the rivers turn, we follow.

sayings.name: Where the footprints vanished
sayings.text: The old ones walked beneath these stars. We walk where their footprints have vanished.

sayings.name: Where the herds find grass
sayings.text: Where the herds find grass, there our tents shall stand.

sayings.name: The whole earth is home
sayings.text: Once, we wandered because we had nowhere to stay. Now we wander because the whole earth is home.
sayings.attribution: Vedda saying, as it is said now

biomes.name: Sea
biomes.notes: Tethyan water. Not walkable in the game.

biomes.name: High Snow
biomes.notes: Wind-packed snow above the treeline. Ordinary ground, not an extreme: a person walks on it, and what grows and hunts there is scarce rather than impossible. It is a sub-biome by design -- the game stamps it as a cap on high ground rather than listing it in a map's `seed_biomes`, because a climate palette would hand it an elevation band and turn a third of a map to snow. Nothing is authored to live here yet; the biome exists so the mountains can have a top.

biomes.name: Floating Island
biomes.notes: The island surface itself — glowing moss, prismatic glass herbs, aero-mangrove groves at the edges. Held up by lodestone cores of Permian-irradiated ore. Renderable since the tiles were painted: `sky_island.png` and `sky_underside.png` are sliced into the terrain sheet and carried in TERRAIN_ORDER.

biomes.name: Island Underside
biomes.notes: The inverted world beneath an island, where gravity is warped and rainwater falls upward. Sky coral calcifies here and holds the crumbling rock together; the Asura-tainted gargoyles shelter in it. Renderable since the tiles were painted: `sky_island.png` and `sky_underside.png` are sliced into the terrain sheet and carried in TERRAIN_ORDER.

biomes.name: Sky Water
biomes.notes: Standing water caught on a floating island: rain that fell on the shelf and never reached the ground, held in a hollow of the lodestone rock and spilling off the lip as a fall. Its own biome rather than `river` because a pool with nothing under it is not a river -- it has no source, no mouth, and everything that lives in it was born there.

biomes.name: Open Sky
biomes.notes: The air between islands, worked by gliders and migrants — aero-mantas, sky-faring orcas, ballooning spiderlings. The orca-blimp routes run through it.

biomes.name: Naraka Rifts
biomes.notes: The rift country beyond the portals: sulphurous rivers, blood-warm pools, the twilight zone. Naraka water is not the Saraswati's, so its creatures do not simply swim into a delta — they cross into this realm at a gate. See `crosses_at` on the species themselves; the Dwarka Gate is the established one (settlement_dwarka, event_shadow_pact, event_naraka_portal). A Naraka creature met in this realm should therefore be met near a gate, not spread through ordinary water.

biomes.name: Lava Sea
biomes.notes: The molten surface and scalding shallows of the Ganges Lava Lake, where magma meets ocean. Distinct from the volcanic highlands around it, which are ordinary mountains and remain renderable. Renderable since the engine gained placeholder tiles: a biome with no drawn art is now drawn from its own colour and symbol rather than being undrawable, so the 29 encounterable fauna and 7 flora that live here can finally be met. The sky biomes and the underworld stay unrenderable because every species in them is authored `lore` -- that is an authorial decision, not a missing drawing.
